full_judgment: 7. Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the contention of the opposite party that the Medical Certificate is inadmissible, is not correct and the learned Subordinate Judge should have allowed commission on consideration of medical certificate. Mr. Asrarul Hussain, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party however, submits that the medical certificate by itself is not evidence unless it is proved by the testimony of the person who granted it. In support of his submissions the learned Advocate refers to a decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Zeauddin Haider Vs Jane Alam, 21 D.L.R. 275. This decision supports the contention of the learned Advocate that the medical certificate is not admissible unless the Doctor giving the certificate is duly examined. In this case a Division Bench took the view that no reliance should be placed on the medical certificate unless the doctor is examined in view of the fact that the allegation of illness was seriously challenged. The learned Judges further held that opportunity for examining the doctor should be given before disposal of such an application. The above view has been taken on the authority of two decisions of the Calcutta High Court, namely, Sris Chandra Nandi Vs Annapurna Roy, A.I.R. 1950 Cal. 173: Panchanan Ghose Vs Bhaggu Bari A.I.R. 1950 Cal. 261. The learned Advocate also refers to a decision of the Supreme Court of India, Ptlad. Tyurkey Read Die Works Company Ltd. Vs. Dyes Chemical Workers Union and others A.I.R. 1960 (S.C.) 1006. There is an observation to the effect that "if a person is to prove that he was ill on that particular (late, the mere filing of certificate of medical man that he was ill on that (late is not accepted as evidence to show that he was ill. The correctness of the statement made in certificate is to be proved by an affidavit or oral testimony in Court by doctor concerned or by some other evidence."
